messages.subject_clean: Question on Sleep Log and Part 4 Output vs Part 5 Output
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have been testing the use of an advanced sleep log with a few files from a study I work on. My sleep log has some missingness due to participants not completing sleep logs for each night worn. GGIR correctly uses the HDZCA algorithm on missing sleep log nights. However, in my output "part4_nightsummary_sleepcleaned," no nights that used the HDZCA algorithm to identify a guider was included in this file, only nights where a sleeplog was available. My part5_daysummary_MM_...." file does include ALL days, both the HDZCA and sleeplog nights.

I was just wondering why there is a discrepancy between these output files? We likely won't use the part4 files as physical activity, not sleep, are our main outcomes, but I just would like to understand why there is a discrepancy for future studies or if the PI requests sleep data.

Thank you,

Reagan

messages.body_plain:
I wouldn't call it a "discrepancy", per se, but rather a "feature" of the distinct (yet overlapping) GGIR Parts 4 and 5.

I am familiar with the scenario you are describing. We had to wrap our minds around it in the past. The GGIR developers have also imagined such a scenario, i.e., recordings with a mixture of sleeplog nights and non-sleeplog nights. The topic is touched on in these two links:

- https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIR.html#565_Difference_between_cleaned_and_full_output
- https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/GGIR.pdf (g.report.part4 description, page 30 in the 3.0-9 PDF)

A salient quote: "In other words, *_cleaned.csv is perfect if you only want to rely on nights with a sleeplog or if you do not use a sleeplog at all. For all other scenarios we advise using the *_full.csv [in QC folder] report and to clean it yourself."

Hope that helps!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,
Thanks for your help with this. I've re-run the script as you suggested and a couple of things jump out.

When looking at the visuals it seems that there is a pretty good distinction between wear and non-wear time across all participants. For the majority of participants the day seems fine and the entirety of every night seems to be classified as non-wear (as we'd expect given we had a waking-wear protocol). I've attached the visual outputs for two participants.

However, when looking at the part 5 outputs things are a bit different. It seems that some participants may have a very small amount of sleep detected in part 4 for some reason, in which case those days are included in the part 5 output, whereas all other participants are excluded from the part 5 outputs. For example, from the two participants in the visual attached, night 3 for the participant 1 has a part 4, and subsequently a part 5 output, but all other days are excluded and participant 2 isn't included at all.

When looking at the part 5 QC output, participants excluded from the main part 5 output also don't have a part 5 QC output. However for the few participants that are included in the main results we get each day in the QC folder. For some reason though it seems that the other days are detected as 100% non-wear. Again, I've attached the QC output for participant 1, the yellow row is the day that is included in the main part 5 output, all other days seem to be classified as 100% non-wear for some reason.

Any ideas on how to solve this would be appreciated.

Regards,
Aaron

Hi Marga,

Yes you can do this. There are some unnecessary steps here but this is what I was doing if I was wanting to re-run parts 3 and 4 to generate a new report with different thresholds for sleep:
1. Copy the part4 results elsewhere.
2. delete config.csv file in output_x
3. Delete ms3.out and ms4.out folders in the output_x/meta folder (leave basic, ms1.out, ms2..out folders)
4. Delete part4 output files in output_x/results folder.
5. change GGIR script to mode=c(3,4) and do.report=c(4), and overwrite=T, then any other functions you want to change e.g. anglethreshold, timethreshold for different parameters.
6. re-run the GGIR script.
7. new meta files and results will be generated based on the newer parameters.

The majority (if not all) of the above isn't necessary if you just include overwrite = TRUE in the GGIR call,  so most of the steps described are just how I do it to make sure that anything I don't want overwriting is copied elsewhere before inadvertently replacing it and having to re-generate.

Thanks,
Ben

messages.subject: Re: Maximum number of files to run?
messages.subject_clean: Maximum number of files to run?
messages.body_plain:
There isn't a limit as with do.parallel=T it will run ncores-1 files at a time e.g. if you have 8 cores it will process 7 files at once and I believe it's recommended to have ~2gb per file in parallel. You could use the maxNcores and try a lower number if you find your PC is struggling to run at the default max number of cores. If that's not helping then someone else may need to chip in with a suggestion or I would be just suggesting that you run 100 files at once e.g. f0=1 and f1=100, then re-run with f0=101 and f1=200 etc. until you have them all if you are looking for a (potentially) quick workaround to get things processing.

An alternate thing to look at would be tools>memory inside R in case there is some bottleneck there and you just need to increase the allocation to your R session.

Thanks,
Ben

messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Re: Maximum number of files to run?
messages.body_plain:
Could it be that you have one or more very large files, which are no part of your test run with 100 files? I have had that issue with some ActiGraph gt3x files which had a lot of sporadic idle sleep mode periods, which can eat a lot of memory.

In that case I recommend:
Move the largest files out of your data folder
Process all your data as you normally do
Move the largest files back
Set do.parallel = FALSE and overwrite = FALSE
Run your R script again, this should then only process the large files.

Another issue I had in the past was that memory per core ratio was too low, which I fixed by installing extra memory in my machine.

Best,

Vincent

Our study protocol defines an adherent wear day as 17hrs of wear in a 24hr period. To that end, I have specified includedaycrit = 17 as a parameter in the code. Thanks in advance.

messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Skeptical about result in sleep duration
messages.body_plain:
Dear Marga,

Very good that you are sceptical, everyone should be sceptical about these implementations. I discussed this in the vignette https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIR.html#561_Notes_on_sleep_classification_algorithms_designed_for_count_data

There are essentially multiple challenges:

Motionlogger Counts: Sadeh and Cole-Kripke used the Motionlogger but they as well as the manufacturer provided no complete transparency about how these counts are calculated. Note that their calculation cannot be the same as the ActiGraph counts used by ActiLife, because they reported to use a zero-crossing counts while ActiGraph count use an area under the curve algorithm. The problem however is that manufacturers like ActiGraph, Actiwatch and many others wanted to benefit from the popularity of the Sadeh and Cole-Kripke algorithm but in order to implement them they had to make some adjustments to their own count values in order to make the algorithm work. Those adjustments are proprietary and have to my knowledge never been shared. As a result, in open source software such as GGIR we have no other choice then to guess how to derive counts with modern data in a way that mimics the counts as used by Sadeh and Cole-kripke in the 1990s.
Orientation of axis: Sadeh reported to use the y-axis without documenting what direction the y-axis points in.
Algorithm itself: Although the algorithm was published, it is not clear whether ActiGraph, Actiwatch and other companies use the exact same algorithm or a slightly revised version of it to improve performance. Without transparency on their side this is hard to verify.
Lack of commitment by sleep research community in the past 30 years to demand transparency from software providers. I have tried to make an educated guess in GGIR based on the information I could find to see how far that would bring us. Further, I did it to educate the research community that claiming to use 1990s algorithms is just a marketing trick by the wearable sensor companies and a completely meaningless way to do science on modern data as it is not transparent.

I welcome efforts to help improve GGIR's implementation of the zero-crossing count and Sadeh and Cole-Kripke algorithms.

Kind regards,

Vincent

Hi Benjamin,

Part 5 is designed to only care about the wear time during waking hours of the day.
At the moment we do not have the functionality you require. Also what you require would only work for MM-window definition.

Possible workarounds:
Use percentage of nonwear in part 5 daysummary output to remove the days you do not want to keep. Probably easiest to automate this with an R script. If you depend on part 5 person level output then you would have to generate that yourself.
Work with GGIR parameter data_cleaning_file, which allows you to specify what days to ignore for each individual in part 5. I imagine this will be more labour intensive.
If you are familiar with R then you could try to write a script that reads and modifies the actual part 5 milestone data output (.RData files), after which you can run GGIR(do.report=5, mode = c()) to regenerate the day and person-level reports. It is a hack and not the most elegant solution though.

Best,

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Yes, counts are now also supported, although it is relatively new and requires a bit more critical attention from users to help spot problems, if any.

See https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIRParameters.html
and then specifically parameter documentation for:
dataFormat
extEpochData_timeformat

When you type ?GGIR inside RStudio console and then scroll down in the documentation you will see examples for different count formats, which I have copy-pasted below. Obviously the specific parameter values need to be tailored to your specific study setting:

       # For externally derived Actiwatch data in .AWD format:
       GGIR(datadir = "/media/actiwatch_awd", # folder with epoch level .AWD file
          outputdir = "/media/myoutput",
          dataFormat = "actiwatch_awd",
          extEpochData_timeformat = "%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S",
          mode = 1:5,
          do.report = c(2, 4, 5),
          windowsizes = c(60, 900, 3600), # 60 is the expected epoch length
          visualreport = FALSE,
          outliers.only = FALSE,
          overwrite = TRUE,
          HASIB.algo = "Sadeh1994",
          def.noc.sleep = c()) # <= because we cannot use HDCZA for ZCY

       # For externally derived Actiwatch data in .CSV format:
       GGIR(datadir = "/media/actiwatch_csv", # folder with epoch level .AWD file
          outputdir = "/media/myoutput",
          dataFormat = "actiwatch_csv",
          extEpochData_timeformat = "%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S",
          mode = 1:5,
          do.report = c(2, 4, 5),
          windowsizes = c(15, 900, 3600), # 15 is the expected epoch length
          visualreport = FALSE,
          outliers.only = FALSE,
          HASIB.algo = "Sadeh1994",
          def.noc.sleep = c()) # <= because we cannot use HDCZA for ZCY

       # For externally derived UK Biobank data in .CSV format:
       GGIR(datadir = "/media/ukbiobank",
           outputdir = "/media/myoutput",
           dataFormat = "ukbiobank_csv",
           extEpochData_timeformat = "%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S",
           mode = c(1:2),
           do.report = c(2),
           windowsizes = c(5, 900, 3600), # We know that data was stored in 5 second epoch
           desiredtz = "Europe/London", # We know that data was collected in the UK
           visualreport = FALSE,
           overwrite = TRUE)

       # For externally derived ActiGraph count data in .CSV format assuming
       # a study protocol where sensor was not worn during the night:
       GGIR(datadir = "/examplefiles",
           outputdir = "",
           dataFormat = "actigraph_csv",
           mode = 1:5,
           do.report = c(2, 4, 5),
           windowsizes = c(5, 900, 3600),
           threshold.in <http://threshold.in> = round(100 * (5/60), digits = 2),
           threshold.mod = round(2500 * (5/60), digits = 2),
           threshold.vig = round(10000 * (5/60), digits = 2),
           extEpochData_timeformat = "%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S",
           do.neishabouricounts = TRUE,
           acc.metric = "NeishabouriCount_x",
           HASPT.algo = "NotWorn",
           HASIB.algo = "NotWorn",
           do.visual = TRUE,
           includedaycrit = 10,
           includenightcrit = 10,
           visualreport = FALSE,
           outliers.only = FALSE,
           save_ms5rawlevels = TRUE,
           ignorenonwear = FALSE,
           HASPT.ignore.invalid = FALSE,
           save_ms5raw_without_invalid = FALSE)

       # For externally derived Sensear data in .xls format:
        GGIR(datadir = "C:/yoursenseweardatafolder",
            outputdir = "D:/youroutputfolder",
            mode = 1:5,
            windowsizes = c(60, 900, 3600),
            threshold.in <http://threshold.in> = 1.5,
            threshold.mod = 3,
            threshold.vig = 6,
            dataFormat = "sensewear_xls",
            extEpochData_timeformat = "%d-%b-%Y %H:%M:%S",
            HASPT.algo = "NotWorn",
            desiredtz = "America/New_York",
            overwrite = TRUE,
            do.report = c(2, 4, 5),
            visualreport = FALSE)

> Dear Marga,
>
> Very good that you are sceptical, everyone should be sceptical about these implementations. I discussed this in the vignette https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIR.html#561_Notes_on_sleep_classification_algorithms_designed_for_count_data
>
> There are essentially multiple challenges:
>
> Motionlogger Counts: Sadeh and Cole-Kripke used the Motionlogger but they as well as the manufacturer provided no complete transparency about how these counts are calculated. Note that their calculation cannot be the same as the ActiGraph counts used by ActiLife, because they reported to use a zero-crossing counts while ActiGraph count use an area under the curve algorithm. The problem however is that manufacturers like ActiGraph, Actiwatch and many others wanted to benefit from the popularity of the Sadeh and Cole-Kripke algorithm but in order to implement them they had to make some adjustments to their own count values in order to make the algorithm work. Those adjustments are proprietary and have to my knowledge never been shared. As a result, in open source software such as GGIR we have no other choice then to guess how to derive counts with modern data in a way that mimics the counts as used by Sadeh and Cole-kripke in the 1990s.
> Orientation of axis: Sadeh reported to use the y-axis without documenting what direction the y-axis points in.
> Algorithm itself: Although the algorithm was published, it is not clear whether ActiGraph, Actiwatch and other companies use the exact same algorithm or a slightly revised version of it to improve performance. Without transparency on their side this is hard to verify.
> Lack of commitment by sleep research community in the past 30 years to demand transparency from software providers. I have tried to make an educated guess in GGIR based on the information I could find to see how far that would bring us. Further, I did it to educate the research community that claiming to use 1990s algorithms is just a marketing trick by the wearable sensor companies and a completely meaningless way to do science on modern data as it is not transparent.
>
> I welcome efforts to help improve GGIR's implementation of the zero-crossing count and Sadeh and Cole-Kripke algorithms.
>
> Kind regards,

Dear Abdul,

I am not sure it is fair to expect from me to provide guidance on this. It is the sleep research community who has been using these methods for decades without ensuring a reproducible description. So, it is the sleep research community that needs to answer these questions.

GGIR is open source research software, which means that I implement a lot of methods as good as I can, even methods that are more experimental or for which it is not entirely clear how the original developer intended them to be implemented. It is not fair to expect from me to take responsibility for the fact that others are not transparent in their work. I have been doing my best to provide value, and I have been trying to encourage researchers that have used these methods to help improve them, but that is all I can do.

Thanks,

Vincent

  # Target sampling frequency (600 measures per minute)

  # Resample the data
  resampled_data <- resample(data, original_sampling_frequency, target_sampling_frequency)
